questions.question: Vaccine immunology.
questions.question_raw: Vaccines

parts.text: Why are live vaccines more effective than inactivated?
Why are conjugated more effective that polysaccharide?

parts_raw.text: Why are live vaccines more effective than inactivated?
Why are conjugated more effective that polysaccharide?

questions.model_answer:
a) Live attenuated vaccines replicate in the host, so antigen is presented over time, at the natural portal of entry, and in the endogenous (MHC class I) pathway as well as class II. This generates both antibody and CD8 cytotoxic plus CD4 helper T-cell responses, mucosal IgA, and durable memory, usually after one or two doses and without adjuvant. Inactivated antigen is a single non-replicating bolus processed mainly through MHC class II, giving predominantly humoral immunity that wanes and requires multiple doses and adjuvant.
b) Pure polysaccharide is a T-cell-independent type 2 antigen: it cross-links B-cell receptors only, so there is no germinal centre reaction, no class switching beyond IgM/IgG2, no affinity maturation, no memory, no boosting (and hyporesponsiveness on repeat dosing), poor immunogenicity under 2 years of age, and no effect on nasopharyngeal carriage. Conjugating the polysaccharide to a carrier protein (CRM197, tetanus/diphtheria toxoid, OMP) makes it T-cell dependent: the B cell internalizes the conjugate and presents carrier peptides on MHC class II to CD4 T cells, producing germinal centres, IgG class switching, affinity maturation, long-lived memory with an anamnestic response, immunogenicity in infants, and reduced carriage with herd protection.

cohort_answer.text: Live vaccines: can stimulate phagocytes (like inactivated) but also stimulate T cells, preventing additional bacterial growth and providing life-long memory. Conjugated vaccines: stimulate a T cell response (not just B cell) via hapten, promoting longer-lived cellular immunity rather than just humoral.

questions.question: Conjugate vaccines.
questions.question_raw: Conjugate vaccine

parts.text: What is it?
What kind of immune response does it elicit?

parts_raw.text: What is it?
What kind of immune response does it elicit?

questions.model_answer:
a) A vaccine in which a poorly immunogenic capsular polysaccharide antigen is covalently linked to an immunogenic carrier protein (CRM197, tetanus or diphtheria toxoid, or meningococcal OMP) - for example Hib, pneumococcal (Pneu-C-13/15/20) and meningococcal conjugate vaccines.
b) A T-cell-dependent response: the polysaccharide-specific B cell internalizes the conjugate and presents carrier-derived peptides on MHC class II to CD4 helper T cells, driving germinal centre formation, IgG class switching, affinity maturation, and long-lived memory B cells with an anamnestic (boostable) response. It is immunogenic in infants under 2 years and reduces nasopharyngeal carriage, giving herd protection - unlike plain polysaccharide, which is T-cell independent, B-cell only, non-boostable and ineffective in infants.

cohort_answer.text: Vaccine antigen bound (conjugated) to a protein carrier to elicit strong response (e.g. HiB conjugated to diphtheria/tetanus toxin; also S. pneumo, N. meningitidis vaccines). Immune response: invokes T cell response - carrier peptide loaded on MHC produces strong T cell response, unlike unconjugated polysaccharide (T cell independent, B cell only); longer lasting with future rapid response

questions.question: Live versus inactivated and protein versus polysaccharide vaccines.

parts.text: Why is a live vaccine better than an inactivated vaccine?

What is the most likely complication from the measles-mumps-rubella-varicella (MMRV) vaccine?

parts_raw.text: Why is live vaccine better than inactivated?

questions.model_answer:
a) A live attenuated vaccine replicates in the host and presents the full array of native antigens in a manner that closely mimics natural infection. It therefore induces both humoral and cell-mediated (CD8/CTL) immunity, at mucosal as well as systemic sites, producing a stronger, broader and more durable response — often protective after one or two doses, without adjuvant and usually without repeated boosters.

b) Polysaccharide antigens are T-cell–independent: they stimulate B cells directly, generating a short-lived IgM-predominant response with no germinal centre reaction, no immunologic memory, no booster (anamnestic) effect, hyporesponsiveness on repeat dosing, and poor immunogenicity in children under 2 years. Conjugating the polysaccharide to a carrier protein converts it to a T-cell–dependent antigen: T-follicular helper cells drive class switching to IgG, affinity maturation and memory B-cell formation, giving durable immunity, a boostable response, immunogenicity in infants, and reduction of nasopharyngeal carriage with herd protection.

c) Febrile seizure. MMRV carries roughly double the risk of febrile seizure of separately administered MMR + varicella (about one extra febrile seizure per 2300–2600 doses) when given as the first dose at 12–23 months, peaking 5–12 days after vaccination. Other adverse events include fever, rash, arthralgia, lymphadenopathy, and rarely ITP.

questions.question_raw: Q10 (2012 PM). Dukoral for traveler's diarrhea

parts.text: Explain the mechanism of action.
What do you need to know to determine how efficacious it would be for each traveller?
What proportion of travellers' diarrhea is caused by enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli?

parts_raw.text: A) Explain mechanism of action

questions.model_answer: a) Dukoral is an oral killed whole-cell Vibrio cholerae O1 vaccine combined with recombinant cholera toxin B subunit. It induces mucosal secretory IgA in the gut: anti-whole-cell antibodies are vibriocidal and block colonization, while anti-CTB antibodies prevent the B subunit from binding GM1 ganglioside on the enterocyte, so the A subunit cannot enter to ADP-ribosylate Gs-alpha, activate adenylate cyclase, raise cAMP and drive CFTR-mediated chloride and water secretion. Because the heat-labile toxin of enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli is structurally and immunologically similar to cholera toxin, anti-CTB antibody gives partial cross-protection against heat-labile-toxin-producing ETEC only - not against heat-stable-toxin-only strains or other pathogens. b) You need: the destination and season (which determines the local prevalence of ETEC versus Campylobacter, Shigella, Salmonella, norovirus and parasites), the duration and style of travel and food/water exposure, the traveller's age (licensed from 2 years) and ability to complete the 2-3 dose series more than 1 week before departure, host factors making illness consequential (achlorhydria/proton pump inhibitor use, inflammatory bowel disease, immunosuppression, prior severe or recurrent travellers' diarrhea, a trip in which brief illness would be intolerable), and realistic expectations of efficacy - roughly 60-85% against cholera but only about 25% against ETEC and under 10% against all-cause travellers' diarrhea, with protection lasting about 3 months. Food and water precautions plus a self-treatment antibiotic and loperamide remain the mainstay. c) ETEC causes roughly 25-50% of travellers' diarrhea overall (varies markedly by destination and season; higher in Latin America and Africa, lower in South and Southeast Asia where Campylobacter predominates).
questions.beyond_mandell: Efficacy figures and traveller selection follow the CATMAT/Canadian Immunization Guide and ISTM/IDSA travellers' diarrhea guidance.

cohort_answer.text: A) Dukoral is a killed whole-cell oral vaccine with the nontoxic B subunit of cholera toxin, providing limited (<50%) protection against ETEC. CtxA cleaved into subunits activates G-protein coupled adenylyl cyclase increasing cAMP, activating chloride/water secretion via CFTR; CTxB binds GM1 receptors; antibodies against CTxB provide cross protection for ETEC toxin. B) Vaccine efficacy against all-cause diarrhea ~6%; protection against O1 Vibrio cholerae 64-85%; protection against ETEC ~25%; limited value, consider for selected high-risk short-term travellers >2 years (chronic illness, increased acquisition risk, immunosuppressed, hx repeated severe TD, brief illness intolerable). C) ETEC accounts for 25-50% of traveler's diarrhea (depends on destination).

questions.model_answer: The serogroup B capsule is alpha(2-8)-linked polysialic acid, structurally identical to polysialylated neural cell adhesion molecule on human fetal and neuronal tissue. It is therefore poorly immunogenic (tolerance to self) and raising antibody carries a theoretical risk of autoimmunity, so capsule-based conjugate vaccines are not feasible. Vaccines instead had to be built from subcapsular protein antigens (outer membrane vesicles, factor H binding protein, NadA, NHBA), which are antigenically variable and strain-specific, so coverage depends on circulating strains and must be estimated by assays such as MATS rather than by serogroup alone.

cohort_answer.text: Antigenic mimicry of the serogroup B polysaccharide capsule, which is composed of polysialic acid structures similar to those expressed on human neuronal cells.

questions.model_answer:
a) Shingrix - recombinant glycoprotein E subunit (non-live, inactivated); adjuvanted with AS01B (MPL + QS-21 in liposomes); 2 doses IM 2-6 months apart; efficacy 96.6%-97.4% against zoster in adults 50-69 years (91.3% in >=70 y) and 88.5%-91.2% against postherpetic neuralgia.
Zostavax II - live attenuated Oka/Merck strain, high titer (~19,400 PFU/dose); no adjuvant; 1 dose subcutaneously; efficacy ~51% against zoster and 67% against PHN, higher in the 60-69 y group than in those >=70 y, with waning after ~8 years.
ACIP recommends Shingrix at >=50 years and prefers it over Zostavax, including in prior Zostavax recipients - so this 60-year-old should receive Shingrix.
questions.beyond_mandell: The AS01B adjuvant composition and the 2-6 month IM dosing interval are from the product monograph/ACIP 2018; the chapter states only that Shingrix is adjuvanted and given as two doses.

cohort_answer.text:
SHINGRIX | Recombinant | Yes (AS01B) | 2 | >90%
ZOSTAVAX II | Live | None | 1 | 50%
Mechanism of Action of AS01B Adjuvant: AS01B adjuvant induces a local and transient activation of the innate immune system by two immune enhancers: MPL, which signals through Toll-like Receptor 4, and QS-21 signaling which involves activity of the NLRP3 inflammasome complex. These two agonists activate antigen presenting cells loaded with antigen in the draining lymph node that enables recruitment of naive CD4+ T cells. Both MPL and QS-21 are required to induce the maximal frequencies of gE-specific cytokine-producing CD4+ T cells and the highest titers of gE-specific antibodies.

questions.model_answer:
Give household-contact PEP as soon as possible (effective within 14 days of exposure): (1) Pregnant wife (healthy adult): single dose of hepatitis A vaccine; pregnancy is not a contraindication. (2) 9-month-old (<12 mo): immune globulin 0.1 mL/kg IM — vaccine is not used for PEP under 12 months. (3) 15-month-old (≥12 mo, healthy): single dose of hepatitis A vaccine.
Return to India: No vaccine needed — natural HAV infection confers lifelong immunity; second attacks are not documented.
Sister (one dose 9 years ago): only 1 additional (second) dose is required, not a restart of the series. The first dose does not need to be repeated regardless of the interval; the series is simply completed, and a robust anamnestic response is expected.

b) He had Pneu-C-7 only. Give a dose of conjugate vaccine (Pneu-C-15 or -20; if 13/15 used, follow with Pneu-P-23 at least 8 weeks later), and give a single Pneu-P-23 booster 5 years after the first Pneu-P-23. questions.model_answer:
a) Both are the same live attenuated Oka strain, but the zoster vaccine contains a far higher titre - about 19,400 PFU per dose versus 1350 PFU for monovalent varicella vaccine (9800 PFU for MMRV) - because a high titre is needed to boost waning cell-mediated immunity in older adults rather than to prime a naive host.
b) Varicella vaccine - two doses; she is susceptible and non-pregnant. Zoster vaccine is not indicated in a VZV-naive person.
c) Herpes zoster vaccine - he is VZV-immune and >=50 years; give recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix), 2 doses.
d) Varicella vaccine - despite her age, she has no evidence of immunity, so she needs primary varicella immunization (2 doses), not zoster vaccine.
e) Advantages of recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) over the live vaccine: (1) Much higher efficacy - 96.6%-97.4% at 50-69 y and 91.3% at >=70 y, versus ~51%, with 88.5%-91.2% protection against PHN; efficacy is preserved in the very elderly, whereas live vaccine efficacy falls with age. (2) Non-live, adjuvanted subunit vaccine, so it carries no risk of vaccine-strain disease and can be used in immunocompromised patients in whom the live vaccine is contraindicated. (3) More durable protection - live vaccine protection wanes after ~8 years, and Shingrix is ACIP-preferred and can be given to previous Zostavax recipients.

questions.model_answer: a) The serogroup B capsule is an (α2→8)-linked polysialic acid that closely resembles human neural cell adhesion molecule (NCAM) and other host antigens; it is therefore poorly immunogenic and carries a theoretical risk of autoimmunity, so it cannot be used as a capsular vaccine target (unlike A/C/W/Y). MenB vaccines instead use semiconserved surface proteins identified by reverse vaccinology (FHbp, NadA, NHBA) ± a PorA-containing outer membrane vesicle preparation (e.g., Bexsero/MenB-4C, Trumenba/MenB-FHbp). b) Indicated for persons ≥10 years at increased risk: (1) persistent (terminal) complement component deficiencies, including those on eculizumab; (2) anatomic or functional asplenia; (3) microbiologists routinely exposed to N. meningitidis isolates; (4) persons at risk during a serogroup B outbreak (e.g., college campuses); also considered in HIV. Routine use is permissive in adolescents/young adults aged 16–23 (preferred 16–18).

questions.model_answer:
Indications (ACIP, per Table 199.7): (1) all adults aged >=65 years; (2) immunocompetent adults 19-64 with chronic conditions - chronic heart disease, chronic lung disease, diabetes, alcoholism, chronic liver disease/cirrhosis, cigarette smoking, CSF leak, cochlear implant; (3) functional/anatomic asplenia (sickle cell, splenectomy); (4) immunocompromising conditions - congenital/acquired immunodeficiency, HIV, chronic renal failure/nephrotic syndrome, leukemia/lymphoma/Hodgkin/generalized malignancy/multiple myeloma, iatrogenic immunosuppression, solid organ transplant; plus routine childhood immunization.

Adults with immunocompromise, asplenia, CSF leak or cochlear implant - PCV13 first, then PPSV23 >=8 weeks later, with PPSV23 revaccination 5 years after the first PPSV23 dose (and, for age <65 groups, a final dose at 65).

questions.model_answer:
a) Yes. For infants 6-11 months travelling to an area of measles risk, give one early dose of measles-containing vaccine (MMR) before departure.
b) Persisting transplacental maternal antibody can neutralize the vaccine virus, and the infant immune system is relatively immature, so seroconversion rates are lower than after 12 months; this early dose therefore does not count toward the routine schedule.

questions.model_answer:
a) Both use the live attenuated Oka strain, but the live zoster vaccine contains a far higher potency of virus (roughly 14-fold or more plaque-forming units per dose) than the varicella vaccine, since it must boost pre-existing VZV cell-mediated immunity rather than prime a naive host.
b) Varicella vaccine, 2 doses 4-8 weeks apart (pregnancy avoided for 1 month after).
c) Recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix), 2 doses 2-6 months apart; no varicella serology needed.
d) Varicella vaccine 2 doses (she is susceptible, so primary varicella immunization takes priority); zoster vaccine is not indicated in a seronegative person.
e) (1) Much higher and more durable efficacy (>90% across all age groups, including >=70 years, with sustained protection beyond 7-10 years versus waning efficacy of the live vaccine). (2) It is non-live, so it can be given safely to immunocompromised patients in whom the live vaccine is contraindicated. (3) Greater efficacy against postherpetic neuralgia and no risk of vaccine-strain disease or need to withhold antivirals; also no cold-chain frozen storage requirement.
questions.beyond_mandell: NACI/ACIP recombinant zoster vaccine recommendations (ZOE-50/ZOE-70 trials).

questions.model_answer: All must be non-live (live vaccines are contraindicated at CD4 <200). (1) Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV20, or PCV15 followed by PPSV23). (2) Hepatitis B vaccine — high/double-dose or adjuvanted schedule, with post-vaccination anti-HBs testing. (3) Hepatitis A vaccine. (4) Quadrivalent meningococcal conjugate vaccine (Men-C-ACYW), 2-dose primary series with boosters, plus MenB vaccine. (5) Inactivated seasonal influenza vaccine, annually. (6) Tdap/Td (with subsequent Td boosters) and inactivated polio vaccine as needed for primary series completion. (7) HPV vaccine (9-valent, 3-dose schedule). Also indicated: recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix, non-live) and COVID-19 vaccine; Haemophilus influenzae type b conjugate vaccine may be given if not previously immunized. Note that immunogenicity is poor at CD4 <100 — re-immunize or check serology after immune reconstitution on ART.

parts.text: Should you give conjugate, polysaccharide, or both? Explain.

parts_raw.text: Should you give conjugate, polysaccharide, or both? Explain

questions.model_answer: a) Give both. In a previously unimmunized asplenic adult, administer the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13) first, followed at least 8 weeks later by the polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23). The conjugate vaccine overcomes the splenic dependence of the antipolysaccharide response (T-cell-dependent, better magnitude/durability and immune memory), while PPSV23 is then added to broaden serotype coverage. Revaccinate with PPSV23 once, 5 years after the first PPSV23 dose (for adults up to age 65).

Why is it not recommended for age < 24 months?

questions.model_answer:
a) LAIV replicates in the nasopharyngeal mucosa and induces local secretory IgA plus cell-mediated and cross-reactive immunity, which in early trials gave superior efficacy to inactivated vaccine in young children; it also requires no needle, improving acceptability and uptake. NACI no longer states a preferential recommendation over inactivated vaccine — either LAIV or IIV may be used in children 2–17 years, and LAIV remains a reasonable option in this age group.

b) Intranasal spray (0.1 mL into each nostril).

c) No. Egg allergy of any severity is not a contraindication to influenza vaccine, including LAIV; residual ovalbumin content is negligible and vaccine may be given in any setting without special precautions or prior skin testing.

d) Because of a small but statistically significant excess of medically attended wheezing and hospitalization in the 2–4 weeks after vaccination in children under 24 months.

e) (1) Immunocompromising conditions or immunosuppressive therapy (including household setting requiring a protective environment). (2) Severe asthma — current active wheezing, or on high-dose/oral corticosteroids, or medically attended wheezing within the previous 7 days. (3) Children and adolescents 2–17 years on chronic acetylsalicylic acid therapy (Reye syndrome risk). (4) Pregnancy. Also: history of Guillain-Barré syndrome within 6 weeks of a previous influenza vaccine. Precautions: significant nasal congestion; avoid influenza antivirals from 48 hours before to 2 weeks after; avoid close contact with severely immunocompromised persons for 2 weeks.
questions.beyond_mandell: NACI seasonal influenza statement: LAIV no longer preferentially recommended over IIV in children 2–17; egg allergy is not a contraindication to any influenza vaccine.

cohort_answer.text: A) [Note: outdated - LAIV no longer preferentially recommended over IIV in children 2-17 per NACI review]. B) Intranasal. C) No - only trace amounts of ovalbumin, very low chance of reaction. D) Small but significant increased rate of wheezing 2-4 weeks following vaccination in this age group. E) Immunocompromised; severe asthma (current active wheezing, oral/high-dose inhaled steroids, or medically attended wheezing in past 7 days); children 2-17 on chronic ASA therapy (Reye's syndrome risk); pregnancy (lack of safety data); GBS onset within 6 weeks of prior influenza vaccination without other known cause. Cautions: avoid if significant nasal congestion; avoid close contact with immunocompromised individuals for 2 weeks after vaccine; wait 48h after antivirals before vaccine or 2 weeks after vaccine before antivirals.

questions.question: Meningococcal vaccines.
questions.question_raw: Meningococcal vaccines

parts.text: Which meningococcal vaccines are available in Canada?
What considerations would you have in using them in an outbreak situation?

parts_raw.text: Which are available in Canada?
What considerations would you have in using in an outbreak situation?

questions.model_answer:
a) Three classes. (1) Monovalent serogroup C conjugate (Men-C-C): Menjugate, NeisVac-C — routine infant/toddler programs. (2) Quadrivalent A, C, Y, W-135 conjugate (Men-C-ACYW): Menactra, Menveo, Nimenrix, MenQuadfi — adolescent programs and high-risk groups (asplenia, complement deficiency including eculizumab/ravulizumab, HIV, travellers to the meningitis belt or Hajj, laboratory workers). (3) Serogroup B protein-based: 4CMenB (Bexsero, from 2 months of age) and MenB-fHbp (Trumenba, 10–25 years). A pentavalent MenABCWY (Penbraya) is also licensed. Plain polysaccharide quadrivalent vaccine is largely obsolete in Canada.

b) (1) Identify the outbreak serogroup by culture/PCR typing — this dictates which product is used, and for MenB whether the strain's antigens are predicted to be covered (MATS/gMATS or fHbp typing). (2) Define the outbreak population and age range — product licensure differs by age (Trumenba 10–25 years; Bexsero from infancy; Men-C-ACYW products vary). (3) Vaccination history and need for a booster or a second dose — MenB requires a 2-dose primary series, so protection is not immediate; the outbreak may still be ongoing when doses are due. (4) Timing and logistics: vaccine takes 1–2 weeks to protect, so chemoprophylaxis of close contacts and case-finding remain the immediate control measures; vaccination is for longer-term interruption of transmission. (5) Special populations: pregnancy and breastfeeding (conjugate vaccines may be given when indicated), immunocompromised hosts requiring extra doses, and contraindications/allergy. (6) Public health coordination — vaccine supply, defining the target cohort, and communication.
questions.beyond_mandell: NACI meningococcal vaccine statement; Canadian products include MenQuadfi and pentavalent MenABCWY in addition to those the cohort lists.

cohort_answer.text: A) Conjugated meningococcal C (Men-C-C): Menjugate Liquid, NeisVac-C. Quadrivalent conjugated (Men-C-ACYW): Menactra, Menveo, Nimenrix. Meningococcal B (4CMenB and MenB-fHBP): Bexsero (4CMenB, can start infancy), Trumenba (fHBP, 10-25yo). B) Serogroup causing the outbreak; age of those being vaccinated; vaccination status; pregnancy/breastfeeding status.

questions.model_answer:
a) In the Shingles Prevention Study, Zostavax reduced the incidence of herpes zoster by ~50% (5.4 vs 11.1 cases/1000 person-years) and reduced the incidence of postherpetic neuralgia by ~67% (0.5 vs 1.4 cases/1000 person-years). (By comparison, Shingrix efficacy was ~96.6-97.4% for zoster in ages 50-69 and PHN prevention ~88.5-91.2%.)
b) Neurologic complications of zoster: (1) postherpetic neuralgia; (2) herpes zoster ophthalmicus (with keratitis/sight threat) and Ramsay Hunt syndrome (geniculate ganglion); (3) meningoencephalitis/encephalitis; (4) granulomatous cerebral angiitis causing ischemic stroke (after zoster ophthalmicus); (5) myelitis, motor neuropathy from anterior horn involvement, and Guillain-Barre syndrome.
c) Indications for IV acyclovir (10 mg/kg q8h): immunocompromised host, organ-/sight-threatening or disseminated disease, CNS involvement (encephalitis/myelitis), and inability to tolerate or absorb oral therapy.

cohort_answer.text: A) Zostavax (live attenuated): reduces herpes zoster incidence by 51% and PHN incidence by 67% vs placebo. Shingrix (recombinant): 95% effective preventing herpes zoster, 90-100% effective reducing PHN, longer immunity. B) PHN (most common); herpes zoster ophthalmicus; CNS infection (meningitis, encephalitis); Ramsay-Hunt syndrome; acute retinal necrosis; myelitis, GBS; stroke-like syndrome (cerebral angiitis). C) Any organ-threatening disease; immunocompromise; unable to tolerate PO.

questions.model_answer:
a) Zostavax is a live attenuated (high-titer Oka, ~19,400 PFU/dose) vaccine; Shingrix is an adjuvanted, inactivated recombinant glycoprotein E subunit vaccine given as two doses. Shingrix is more efficacious and ACIP considers it preferable to Zostavax.
b) Zostavax: prevention of herpes zoster in immunocompetent adults (FDA-approved >=50, ACIP recommended >=60). Shingrix: prevention of herpes zoster in adults >=50, two doses, including previous recipients of Zostavax. Neither is indicated to treat established zoster or PHN.
c) Zostavax efficacy wanes with advanced age: it was more effective at preventing zoster in the younger elderly (60-69) than the older elderly (>=70), though it prevented PHN similarly in both groups. Shingrix retains high efficacy even at >=70 (91.3%), declining much less with age.

cohort_answer.text: A) Zostavax: live attenuated vaccine. Shingrix: inactivated (recombinant glycoprotein E vaccine with AS01B adjuvant). RZV superior to ZVL in reducing herpes zoster incidence and PHN in patients >60. B) Zostavax: immunocompetent patients ≥50 without contraindications when Shingrix contraindicated/unavailable; contraindications include immunosuppression, hypersensitivity history, pregnancy, precaution in breastfeeding. Shingrix: ≥50yo without contraindications (including prior Zostavax or zoster episode), immunocompromised adults ≥50yo, post-herpes zoster ≥1 year after episode; 2 doses; contraindications hypersensitivity, precaution in pregnancy/breastfeeding/immunocompromised. C) Zostavax effectiveness declines with advanced age (delayed effectiveness); Shingrix efficacy is higher and declines more slowly with age than Zostavax.

questions.question: Yellow fever vaccine.

parts.text: Side effects of yellow fever vaccine, including the worst one.
What are two contraindications to the yellow fever vaccine?
What do you tell someone going to an endemic area who is not allowed to have the vaccine?

parts_raw.text: A) Side effects of Yellow Fever vaccine (worst one?)
B) What are 2 contraindications to the yellow fever vaccine?
C) What do you tell someone going to an endemic area who is not allowed to have the vaccine?

questions.model_answer:
a) Common/mild: injection site soreness, low-grade fever, headache and myalgia in 10–30%, 5–10 days post-vaccination. Serious: immediate hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis (egg or gelatin, ~1.3/100,000). The two severe syndromes are YEL-AND (vaccine-associated neurotropic disease — meningoencephalitis, ADEM, Guillain-Barré syndrome, bulbar palsy; onset 3–28 days; ~0.8/100,000, higher at the extremes of age; usually recovers) and, the worst, YEL-AVD (vaccine-associated viscerotropic disease — a yellow-fever-like multi-organ failure syndrome with hepatitis, renal failure, coagulopathy and shock, onset 2–5 days after a first dose, ~0.3–0.4/100,000 but higher over age 60, case fatality about 50–65%; associated with thymic disease).

b) (1) Infants under 6 months of age (risk of vaccine-associated encephalitis). (2) Immunosuppression — symptomatic HIV or CD4 <200, hematologic or generalized malignancy, transplant recipients, high-dose corticosteroids or biologics, primary immunodeficiency. Also: thymus disorder (thymoma, thymectomy, myasthenia gravis) and anaphylaxis to egg, chicken protein or gelatin. Precautions: age 6–8 months, age ≥60 years, pregnancy and breastfeeding, asymptomatic HIV with CD4 200–499.

c) (1) Advise deferring or avoiding travel to the yellow fever endemic/transmission area if at all possible, or substituting a non-endemic destination. (2) If travel is unavoidable, emphasize rigorous mosquito bite avoidance against the day-biting Aedes aegypti: DEET or icaridin repellent, permethrin-treated clothing, long sleeves and trousers, air-conditioned or screened accommodation, bed nets, and avoidance of peridomestic standing water. (3) Provide a signed Medical Contraindication to Vaccination waiver on the International Certificate of Vaccination or Prophylaxis, and warn that the destination or a transit country may refuse entry, quarantine the traveller, or vaccinate at the border regardless of the waiver. (4) Counsel on the symptoms of yellow fever and the need to seek medical care promptly, and review other required travel immunizations and malaria chemoprophylaxis.

questions.model_answer:
a) RotaTeq (RV5) is pentavalent, containing five human-bovine reassortants expressing human outer capsid proteins G1, G2, G3, G4 and P1A[8] on a bovine WC3 backbone. Rotarix (RV1) is monovalent, G1P1A[8], and protects heterotypically against G2, G3, G4 and G9 through shared P[8] and cross-reactive immunity.

b) RotaTeq: human-bovine reassortant derived from the bovine strain WC3. Rotarix: attenuated human strain 89-12 (RIX4414), passaged in cell culture.

c) Routine immunization of all healthy infants, to be given as part of the primary infant schedule; particularly important given rotavirus is the leading cause of severe infant gastroenteritis. Also given to preterm infants who are clinically stable, and may be given to infants in hospital with appropriate contact precautions.

d) (1) Anaphylaxis to a vaccine component or a previous dose (RotaTeq contains latex in the applicator; Rotarix oral applicator is latex-containing in some presentations). (2) History of intussusception, or an uncorrected congenital malformation of the gastrointestinal tract predisposing to intussusception (e.g. Meckel diverticulum). (3) Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) — risk of prolonged vaccine-virus shedding and vaccine-associated gastroenteritis. (4) Age outside the licensed window — first dose should not be started at or after 15 weeks and no dose given after 8 months of age. Precautions: moderate to severe acute illness including acute gastroenteritis, chronic gastrointestinal disease, other immunodeficiency or immunosuppressive therapy.

e) Both are given orally only — never injected. RotaTeq: 3 doses of 2 mL at approximately 2, 4 and 6 months. Rotarix: 2 doses of 1.5 mL at approximately 2 and 4 months. For both, the first dose is given between 6 and 14 weeks 6 days of age, doses are a minimum of 4 weeks apart, and the series must be completed by 8 months of age. If a dose is regurgitated it is not repeated. The series should be completed with the same product where possible.

f) Generally well tolerated. Mild irritability, fever, vomiting and diarrhea occur slightly more often than in placebo recipients. The important adverse event is intussusception — an excess of roughly 1 to 5 cases per 100,000 vaccinated infants, concentrated in the 7 days after the first dose; this is far lower than the risk with the withdrawn rhesus reassortant vaccine RotaShield. Vaccine virus is shed in the stool for up to 2–4 weeks, with rare transmission to contacts, and can cause prolonged infection in infants with SCID.

questions.question_raw: Vaccines in HSCT/SOT transplant patients

parts.text: When is the earliest you can give inactivated vaccines pre-transplant?
When is the earliest you can give inactivated vaccines post-transplant?

parts_raw.text: When is the earliest you can give inactivated vaccines pre-transplant?
When is the earliest you can give inactivated vaccines post-transplant?

questions.model_answer:
a) Inactivated vaccines should be given at least 2 weeks before transplant (before the start of conditioning for HSCT, or before transplant/induction immunosuppression for SOT), so that the response is mounted while the patient is still relatively immunocompetent. Live vaccines require a longer interval — at least 4 weeks before conditioning or transplant. Ideally the full indicated schedule is completed during the pre-transplant assessment, as immunogenicity is much better before than after transplant.

b) HSCT: inactivated vaccines are restarted at 3 to 6 months post-transplant — influenza vaccine as early as 3–4 months (or 6 months, with a second dose if given earlier), and the routine re-immunization series (pneumococcal conjugate, Tdap-IPV-Hib, hepatitis B, meningococcal, HPV) generally beginning at 6 months. Live vaccines (MMR, varicella) are deferred to at least 24 months post-transplant and only if the patient is off immunosuppression, free of chronic GVHD, and immunocompetent. SOT: inactivated vaccines are given from 3 to 6 months post-transplant, once maintenance-level immunosuppression is reached and the patient is stable; influenza vaccine may be given as early as 1 month post-transplant during an outbreak or season. Live vaccines are generally contraindicated after SOT. Additional points: hepatitis B at double dose with serologic follow-up, HPV as a 3-dose series regardless of age, and recombinant zoster vaccine (non-live) is safe and indicated in both populations.
questions.beyond_mandell: AST Infectious Diseases Community of Practice vaccination guidelines and NACI Immunization of Immunocompromised Persons.

cohort_answer.text: A) Inactivated vaccines: at least 2 weeks before conditioning. Live attenuated vaccines: at least 4 weeks before conditioning. B) SOT: live vaccines not recommended post-SOT; inactivated vaccine wait 3-6 months post-transplant or when maintenance immunosuppression attained; HepB at double usual dose; HPV 3-dose schedule regardless of age. HSCT: live vaccine around 24 months post-transplant if immunocompetent and no GVHD; inactivated vaccine 6-12 months post-transplant; COVID (3 doses + boosters) can begin 3-6 months post-transplant.

questions.model_answer:
a) Ongoing significant immunosuppression — active chronic GVHD requiring systemic corticosteroids or other immunosuppressive therapy. Such a patient is unlikely to mount a protective response, and live attenuated vaccines (MMR, varicella) remain contraindicated until off immunosuppression and free of GVHD. Recent receipt of IVIG or other antibody-containing blood product is a further reason to defer live measles- and varicella-containing vaccines, for 8 to 11 months depending on the product and dose.

b) Given it is November: (1) Inactivated influenza vaccine, annually, for all household members and close contacts — the single highest-yield cocoon strategy. (2) COVID-19 vaccine, up to date. Other priorities: MMR and varicella for non-immune household members (these live vaccines are safe for contacts, as vaccine virus is not transmitted, except for rare varicella-vaccine rash — cover the rash and avoid contact if it occurs), Tdap for pertussis, and rotavirus for infants in the household (with hand hygiene, as vaccine virus is shed in stool for up to 4 weeks). Household contacts should not receive live attenuated intranasal influenza vaccine or oral polio vaccine if the transplant recipient is severely immunocompromised.

parts.text: Approach to vaccination over the first 2 years post-bone marrow transplant

parts_raw.text: Approach to vaccination over first 2 years post-BMT

questions.model_answer: a) Principle: myeloablation destroys pre-existing immune memory, so all recipients (autologous and allogeneic alike) are treated as never immunized and given a full primary re-immunization series; responses to polysaccharide antigens are poor, so conjugate vaccines are preferred and serology may be checked where available. Pre-transplant, if time permits: age-appropriate inactivated vaccines, conjugate pneumococcal vaccine regardless of age, and inactivated influenza in season, given at least 2 weeks before conditioning; no live vaccine within 4 weeks of starting conditioning. Post-transplant inactivated schedule: inactivated influenza annually starting 4-6 months post-transplant (lifelong); conjugate pneumococcal 3-dose primary series starting 3-6 months, doses at least 4 weeks apart, with a booster at 12-18 months (a polysaccharide or additional conjugate dose at 12-18 months depending on product); diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis (age-appropriate DTaP/Tdap) 3 doses from 6-12 months; Haemophilus influenzae type b conjugate 3 doses from 6-12 months; inactivated polio 3 doses from 6-12 months; hepatitis B 3-4 doses from 6-12 months using high-dose/double-dose product with post-series serology; quadrivalent meningococcal conjugate 2 doses from 6-12 months (and meningococcal B, particularly with GVHD, asplenia, or eculizumab); HPV 3-dose series from 6-12 months in eligible ages; consider hepatitis A, and household/close-contact immunization (cocooning) with inactivated influenza and Tdap. Live vaccines (MMR, varicella) are deferred to 24 months post-transplant and given only if there is no chronic GVHD, immunosuppression has been stopped for more than 3 months, malignancy is in remission, and there is evidence of immune reconstitution; zoster live vaccine is avoided (use recombinant subunit instead). If the patient is receiving IVIG, delay measles- and varicella-containing vaccines by 8-11 months after the last dose. Yellow fever may be considered after 24 months in a reconstituted, non-immunosuppressed traveller to an endemic area. Antimicrobial prophylaxis against encapsulated organisms continues alongside vaccination while immunosuppressed.
questions.beyond_mandell: Schedule follows NACI/CIC Canadian Immunization Guide immunocompromised chapter and IDSA/ASBMT 2013 guidelines for HSCT recipients.

cohort_answer.text: Pre-HSCT: if time permits, give all routine inactivated vaccines appropriate for age, conjugate pneumococcal vaccine regardless of age (ideally Pneu-C-20), polysaccharide pneumococcal if age ≥2 + Pneu-C-13/15, inactivated influenza if flu season; give inactivated vaccines ≥2 weeks before transplant; live vaccines not within 4 weeks of conditioning start. Post-HSCT: treat allogeneic same as autologous; consider all as never immunized and re-immunize (bone marrow ablation eliminates immune memory); poor response to polysaccharide vaccines; measure post-vaccination titres if possible; higher risk for pneumococcus, Hib, measles, varicella, influenza. Schedule: DTP 3 doses from 6-12 months post-HSCT; Hib 3 doses from 6-12 months; HepB 3-4 doses at 6-12 months (double dose); HPV 3 doses at 6-12 months; influenza (inactivated) annually from 4-6 months; quadrivalent meningococcal conjugate 2 doses from 6 months (if asplenic); PNEU-C-20 primary series 3 doses starting 3-9 months (≥4 weeks apart) + booster at 12-18 months; inactivated polio 3 doses at 6-12 months. Live vaccines (MMR, varicella) at 24 months post-BMT if no GVHD, immunosuppression stopped >3 months, disease inactive, and immunocompetent; YF vaccine possible if criteria met and travelling to endemic area; IVIG inactivates live vaccines so delay 8-11 months after last IVIG dose.

questions.question: Two meningococcal serogroups have historically been associated with the Hajj pilgrimage.
questions.question_raw:
Q47 (2009 AM)
2 meningococcal strains associated with Hajj pilgrimage

parts.text: How has vaccination changed this?

parts_raw.text: C) How has vaccination changed this?

questions.model_answer: a) Historically Hajj outbreaks were caused by serogroups A and C, prompting a mandatory A/C polysaccharide vaccine requirement in 1986. After large serogroup W (W-135) outbreaks in 2000-2001, a quadrivalent A, C, Y, W vaccine (polysaccharide within 3 years or conjugate within 5 years) became a requirement for a Hajj/Umrah visa; arrivals from the African meningitis belt also receive ciprofloxacin chemoprophylaxis at entry. As a result, vaccine-serogroup (A, C, W) disease and carriage have fallen dramatically (carriage now <5% in pilgrims, 0-0.6% in returning pilgrims), so residual/emerging disease is now driven by non-vaccine serogroups, chiefly B and serogroup X from the meningitis belt.

cohort_answer.text: Pre-vaccine era, meningitis caused more frequently by 5 serogroups (A, B, C, W-135, Y), with B and C the majority. After vaccine C implementation, serogroup C became rare, more B seen, Y second in Canada. For Hajj, quadrivalent (A,C,Y,W) vaccine mandatory led to more non-vaccine serotypes seen: B (worldwide) and X (from Africa meningitis belt)

questions.model_answer: a) Give a measles-containing vaccine (MMR) now before travel: infants 6-11 months old travelling to a measles-endemic area should receive an early dose, which is safe and offers partial protection, but this dose does not count toward the routine series. b) Two reasons: (1) persisting transplacentally acquired maternal IgG neutralizes vaccine virus and blunts replication; (2) immaturity of the infant immune system - limited B-cell and follicular helper T-cell responses and immature antigen-presenting cell/dendritic cell function - gives a suboptimal humoral response before about 9-12 months. c) Two further doses after the first birthday: the first at 12-15 months and the second at 18 months (or at least 4 weeks after the first if further travel is planned).

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Waning anti-HBs titre in a previous responder (anti-HBs can fall below detection over time although immune memory usually persists). B: Repeat HBsAb, HBsAg, HBcAb and obtain liver enzymes.
